findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Note: one secondary source (pamatnik-terezin summary) erroneously cited Dec 1941; holocaust.cz transport registry confirms Dec 17, 1942.

findings.claim: Number of children taught by Friedl Dicker-Brandeis in clandestine Terezín art classes and survival rate of identified child artists
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Counts vary between ~600 taught (general summaries) and ~660 identified child authors in the surviving suitcase archive (Elena Makarova research), of whom ~550 were murdered in Auschwitz.

findings.claim: Friedl Dicker-Brandeis packing of drawings into two suitcases, deportation to Auschwitz, and date of murder
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Some summaries conflate Oct 6 and Oct 9 as her transport date; holocaust.cz and yadvashem.org confirm Transport Eo-167 departed Terezín on Oct 6, 1944, and auschwitz.at/ushmm.org record her murder on Oct 9, 1944 (some sources note Oct 9–12 upon arrival). She packed two suitcases (entrusted to Raja Engländerová / Willy Groag in girls' home L 410). Her husband Pavel Brandeis survived.
findings.value_or_range: 2 suitcases; deported 1944-10-06 (Transport Eo, No. 167); murdered 1944-10-09 in Auschwitz-Birkenau

findings.claim: Exact count of surviving Terezín children's drawings held by the Jewish Museum in Prague
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Literature cites ~4,000, 4,387, ~4,500, and ~5,000. 4,387 is the exact cataloged drawing count at the Jewish Museum in Prague (inscribed on UNESCO Memory of the World Register); rounded figures (~4,000–4,500 or up to ~5,000) reflect broad estimates or inclusion of collages, two-sided sheets, or non-drawing items.
sources: radio.cz / UNESCO Memory of the World
findings.value_or_range: 4,387 cataloged drawings (commonly rounded in secondary literature to ~4,000–5,000)

findings.claim: Exact count of surviving children's poems held by the Jewish Museum in Prague archive
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Official jewishmuseum.cz summaries verify the 4,387 drawings count but do not publish a single canonical archive-wide poem total in indexed pages; the often-cited '~66+ poems' figure was not independently verified against a JMP archival inventory. Note also that poems such as Pavel Friedmann's typed manuscript were donated separately after the war rather than hidden in Dicker-Brandeis's two suitcases.
findings.value_or_range: Unverified exact archive total (commonly cited as ~66+ poems in secondary summaries; JMP online summaries specify 4,387 drawings alongside unspecified poems/writings)

findings.claim: Publication history of I Never Saw Another Butterfly (Czech first edition and English editions)
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Czech 1st ed.: Dětské kresby na zastávce k smrti, Terezín 1942–1944 (1959, State Jewish Museum in Prague / Hana Volavková ed., epilogue by Jiří Weil). Foreign/export editions by Artia (Prague) began circulating ~1962; first US English edition by McGraw-Hill (1964); UK edition by Neville Spearman (1965, though some listings cite 1962–1965 impressions); Schocken Books editions in 1978 and expanded 2nd edition in 1993 hardcover / 1994 paperback (with USHMM, foreword by Chaim Potok, afterword by Václav Havel). A separate 1993 Jewish Museum in Prague volume titled I Have Not Seen a Butterfly Around Here used multiple translators.
findings.value_or_range: 1959 (Czech, State Jewish Museum Prague) -> 1962 (Artia export/international) -> 1964 (US, McGraw-Hill) -> 1965 (UK, Neville Spearman) -> 1978 & 1993/1994 (US, Schocken Books)

findings.claim: Translator of 'The Butterfly' in I Never Saw Another Butterfly (Jeanne Němcová vs. Edith Pargeter vs. Ewald Osers)
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Jeanne Němcová (Jeanne W. Němcová) is the credited translator of I Never Saw Another Butterfly (1964 McGraw-Hill / 1978 & 1993 Schocken) and specifically of Pavel Friedmann's 'The Butterfly' ('The last, the very last / So richly, brightly, dazzlingly yellow...'). Edith Pargeter (Ellis Peters) did NOT translate I Never Saw Another Butterfly (she translated Josef Bor's The Terezín Requiem in 1963, and contributed to the separate 1993 Prague museum volume I Have Not Seen a Butterfly Around Here alongside Jeanne Němcová and Joy Kadečková). Ewald Osers (1917–2011) translated other Czech poetry (e.g., Seifert, Holub), not Volavková's anthology. An unattributed alternate English translation ('He was the last. Truly the last. / Such yellowness was bitter and blinding...') is used by Holocaust Memorial Day Trust (hmd.org.uk) and Posen Library (posenlibrary.com).
findings.value_or_range: Jeanne Němcová (canonical anthology translation); NOT Edith Pargeter or Ewald Osers

findings.claim: Pavel Friedmann's birth, age when writing 'The Butterfly', and pre-deportation residence
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Despite frequent inclusion in 'children's' Holocaust anthologies, Pavel Friedmann was 21 years old (21 years, 4 months, 28 days) when he wrote 'The Butterfly' on June 4, 1942—an adult young man, not a child.
findings.value_or_range: Born 1921-01-07 in Prague (last residence Prague I, Dlouhá 33); age 21 when writing 'The Butterfly' on 1942-06-04

findings.claim: Pavel Friedmann's deportation to Terezín vs. the 'seven weeks' line in 'The Butterfly'
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: holocaust.cz records Transport Ao, No. 956 departing Prague (assembled at Veletržní palác) on April 28, 1942. Many secondary sources (gov.mb.ca, hmd.org.uk) state April 26, 1942 (likely reflecting assembly/summons date). From April 28 to June 4, 1942 is 37 days (5 weeks, 2 days); from April 26 to June 4 is 39 days (5 weeks, 4 days). Thus the Czech line 'na sedmý týden tu žiji' (literally 'going on the seventh week' / translated as 'For seven weeks I've lived in here') overstates his actual stay by ~1.5 weeks (he was in his 6th week).
findings.value_or_range: Deported 1942-04-28 (Transport Ao, No. 956; secondary sources cite 1942-04-26); 37–39 days in Terezín by 1942-06-04 (in 6th week, not 7 full weeks)

findings.claim: Pavel Friedmann's deportation to Auschwitz and death
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Deported from Terezín to Auschwitz on Sept 29, 1944 via Transport El, No. 95. Secondary sources frequently give Sept 29, 1944 as his death date, but holocaust.cz records him as murdered without confirming an exact day of death in Auschwitz beyond the Sept 29 transport departure (age 23). His typed poem on thin copy paper was donated to the State Jewish Museum in Prague after WWII.
findings.value_or_range: Deported 1944-09-29 (Transport El, No. 95); murdered in Auschwitz (age 23; exact day of death unconfirmed)

findings.claim: Czech/EU public-domain status of Pavel Friedmann's original 1942 Czech poem 'Motýl'
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Under Czech Copyright Act No. 121/2000 Sb. and EU term harmonization (life + 70 years from Jan 1 following death year), Friedmann's 1944 death placed his original Czech works in the public domain in Czechia/EU on January 1, 2015.
findings.value_or_range: Public domain in Czech Republic / EU since 2015-01-01 (1944 + 70 years)

findings.claim: US copyright status of Pavel Friedmann's 1942 Czech poem and Jeanne Němcová's English translation in I Never Saw Another Butterfly
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Direct US Copyright Office registration/renewal records were not retrieved in full. However: (1) Under URAA (17 U.S.C. § 104A), because Pavel Friedmann's Czech text was still protected in Czechia on Jan 1, 1996 (1944+70 = 2014), if first published in the 1959 Prague edition it would have had US copyright restored for 95 years from publication (through Dec 31, 2054; PD Jan 1, 2055), though some repositories treat it as an unpublished archival manuscript or unrenewed work. (2) The English translation by Jeanne Němcová (first US edition 1964; Schocken editions 1978, 1993) remains under copyright in the US (Schocken's 1993 edition explicitly asserts 'Copyright © 1978, 1993 by Artia, Prague. Compilation © 1993 by Schocken Books.') and likely in Czechia/EU as well (Jeanne Němcová was active 1960s–1980s; exact death date undocumented in searched public databases).
findings.value_or_range: English translation under copyright (© 1978, 1993 Artia / © 1993 Schocken; US 95-year term up to 2059–2073); Czech poem's US status depends on 1959 publication vs. URAA restoration (up to 2054)

myths_checked: Myth: Pavel Friedmann was a young child in Friedl Dicker-Brandeis's art class. Verified reality: Friedmann was born Jan 7, 1921, making him 21 years old when he wrote 'The Butterfly' on June 4, 1942 (six months before Friedl Dicker-Brandeis even arrived in Terezín on Dec 17, 1942); his typed poem was donated to the Jewish Museum in Prague after the war, not packed in her suitcases.

Myth: Pavel Friedmann had lived in Terezín for seven full weeks when he wrote 'The Butterfly' on June 4, 1942. Verified reality: Archival transport records (holocaust.cz) date Transport Ao to April 28, 1942 (37 days / 5 weeks 2 days before June 4; secondary sources citing April 26 give 39 days / 5 weeks 4 days)—so 'na sedmý týden' is poetic/imprecise rather than 49 days.

Myth: Edith Pargeter or Ewald Osers translated 'The Butterfly' in I Never Saw Another Butterfly. Verified reality: Jeanne Němcová translated I Never Saw Another Butterfly (1964 McGraw-Hill / 1978 & 1993 Schocken); Pargeter contributed only to a separate 1993 Prague Museum book (I Have Not Seen a Butterfly Around Here) and translated Josef Bor's The Terezín Requiem (1963), while Osers translated other Czech poets.

Myth: Because Pavel Friedmann died in 1944, 'The Butterfly' in English is necessarily in the public domain worldwide. Verified reality: Only Friedmann's 1942 Czech original entered the Czech/EU public domain on Jan 1, 2015 (1944+70); Jeanne Němcová's English translation and the Schocken/Artia editions remain copyrighted in the US (© 1978, 1993 Artia / © 1993 Schocken) and EU, and the Czech poem itself may fall under US URAA restoration (1959+95 = 2054) if first published in 1959.
